OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $H(n)$ be the smallest integer $l$ such that there exist $k<l$ with $(k^n-1,l^n-1)=1$.
Is it true that $H(n)=3$ infinitely often? (That is, $(2^n-1,3^n-1)=1$ infinitely often?)
Estimate $H(n)$. Is it true that there exists some constant $c>0$ such that, for all $\epsilon>0$,\[H(n) > \exp(n^{(c-\epsilon)/\log\log n})\]for infinitely many $n$ and\[H(n) < \exp(n^{(c+\epsilon)/\log\log n})\]for all large enough $n$?
Does a similar upper bound hold for the smallest $k$ such that $(k^n-1,2^n-1)=1$?
#820: [Er74b]
number theory
Erdős [Er74b] proved that there exists a constant $c>0$ such that\[H(n) > \exp(n^{c/(\log\log n)^2})\]for infinitely many $n$.
van Doorn in the comments sketches a proof of the lower bound: that there exists some constant $c>0$ and infinitely many $n$ such that\[H(n) > \exp(n^{c/\log\log n}).\]The sequence $H(n)$ for $1\leq n\leq 10$ is\[3,3,3,6,3,18,3,6,3,12.\]The sequence of $n$ for which $(2^n-1,3^n-1)=1$ is A263647 in the OEIS.
See also [770].
Additional thanks to: Wouter van Doorn

 The proof by Erdős combined with slightly more recent knowledge provides the required lower bound on $H(n)$ for infinitely many $n$, modulo the exact value of the constant $c$. Let me explain.
Let $\omega^*(n)$ count the number of primes $p$ such that $p-1$ divides $n$. By Proposition $10$ in this 1983 paper by Adleman, Pomerance and Rumely (see page $201$, or page $29$ of the pdf-file), there exists an absolute constant $c > 0$ such that there are infinitely many $n$ with $\omega^*(n) > n^{c/\log \log n}$.
So let $n$ be a large enough integer for which $m > n^{c/\log \log n}$ primes $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_m$ exist with $p_i - 1 | n$. With $k < l = H(n)$ such that $\gcd(k^n-1, l^n-1) = 1$, we then must have that $kl$ is divisible by the product $p_1p_2 \cdots p_m$ due to Fermat's little theorem. By noting that this product $p_1p_2\cdots p_m$ is, by the prime number theorem, larger than $e^{2m}$ if $n$ (and therefore $m$) is large enough, we get
\begin{align*}
H(n) &> \sqrt{kl} \\
&\ge \sqrt{p_1p_2 \cdots p_m} \\
&> e^m \\
&> \exp[n^{c/\log \log n}],
\end{align*}as promised.
By the way, since $\omega^*(n)$ is at most the number of divisors of $n$, which is in turn upper bounded by $n^{(\log 2 + o(1))/\log \log n}$, it is tempting to think that the optimal $c$ could be $\log 2$. But I certainly have no idea, and this is pure speculation.

 As it turns out, on the exact same day I originally wrote the above comment, this paper by Fan and Pollack came out. In it, they prove that one can take $c = 0.67 \cdot \log 2$ in the Adleman-Pomerance-Rumely result, and hence in the lower bound here as well. Given the proof claim submitted by Price just yesterday showing that $\log 2 + \varepsilon$ is not admissible, this suddenly gives my $\log 2$ speculation a lot more weight!

claimed by Liam Price (using GPT 5.6 Sol Pro and Claude Fable 5).

 GPT 5.6 Sol Pro proves $H(n)\le K(n)<\exp\bigl(n^{(\log 2+\varepsilon)/\log\log n}\bigr)$ for every $\varepsilon>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$, answering the upper-bound question affirmatively. 
The Lean formalisation was performed by Claude Fable 5.
